Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Kofi had always been drawn to the field of psychology, hoping to make a difference in people's lives. As a psychologist himself, he had spent years honing his skills, working with patients from diverse backgrounds and struggles. But it was one fateful night that would shatter his sense of security and upend his world. It happened during a conference at a downtown hotel. Kofi had stepped out of the bar to grab some fresh air, leaving his drink behind. The next thing he knew, he was being dragged into an empty room by two men. The details of what followed were etched in his mind like a scar – the feeling of suffocation, the sound of laughter, and the smell of cheap cologne. When it was all over, Kofi stumbled out of the room, disoriented and shaken. In the weeks that followed, Kofi began to notice changes in himself. He would feel an overwhelming sense of unease whenever he found himself in locked or confined spaces – elevators, meeting rooms, even his own apartment. The memory of being trapped and helpless would flood back, leaving him breathless and panicked. Comments on sexual violence, whether in conversation or online, would make his skin crawl, as if the words themselves held a malevolent power. Being alone with men became increasingly difficult for Kofi. He couldn't shake off the feeling that they could see right through him, that they knew what had happened. His social life began to suffer as he started avoiding gatherings and events where he might be alone with colleagues or acquaintances. Even in his own practice, working with male patients made him feel uneasy, like he was waiting for them to discover his secret. Kofi's home became a sanctuary, but also a prison. He would position himself with his back against the wall, scanning the room for potential threats. Sleep eluded him as he lay awake, listening for any unusual sounds. Relaxation felt like an impossibility – even in moments of quiet solitude, Kofi's mind would be racing, anticipating the worst. As time passed, these habits solidified into a way of life. Kofi became withdrawn, afraid to venture out or engage with others. His relationships suffered, and his work began to falter. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was walking on thin ice, waiting for the other shoe to drop. One of the most insidious effects of the trauma was the sense of hopelessness that had taken hold. Kofi felt like he was staring into an abyss, with no future or purpose in sight. The helplessness he experienced during the assault had seeped into every aspect of his life – he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him, and so he waited for them to occur. The fear that others could see what happened to him simply by looking at him was a constant companion. Kofi felt exposed, like an open wound, vulnerable to the judgments and scrutiny of those around him. He began to wonder if his patients saw it too – if they knew that their psychologist was broken, just like them. It was this sense of despair, combined with the strain on his relationships and work, that finally brought Kofi to seek help. As he sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't help but feel a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this darkness – a way to reclaim his life, his sense of self, and his future. But for now, the fear of being overwhelmed by his own memories, of losing himself in the abyss of trauma, kept him frozen, waiting for someone to help him find solid ground again.
